A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MEC research. The text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison. Existing material can be matched across the inserted sections, renumbering, and figure relocations.

before.justification: v1 reports original Monte Carlo simulations in Section 6 and Appendices F–G, plus an Energy Efficiency data analysis in Appendix H.

after.justification: v2 retains the original simulations and Energy Efficiency analysis and adds empirical comparisons and weight diagnostics in Appendix G.3, Table 2.

M1.justification: The original mean estimator remains unchanged, but new Appendix B substantially extends the proposed procedure to general weighted estimating equations. Concrete adaptations include separately calibrating propensity-based treatment/control weights for ATE estimation and calibrating external-control weights using survival predictions before solving a weighted Cox score.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same synthetic mean-estimation problems and Energy Efficiency Heating Load application. Table 2 uses an existing synthetic-data setting. The new ATE and survival examples are mathematical constructions, without corresponding empirical evaluations.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds actual comparisons with cross-fitted PPI++ and moment-basis calibration under four generators. These were discussed but not evaluated in v1. Although confined to one KRR setting, this materially expands comparison to an efficiency-tuned PPI competitor and alternative calibration methods.

E3.justification: Appendix G.3 augments evaluation at N = 1000, n = 100 with KRR by reporting RMSE, unnormalized mean CI length, and weight ESS/CV diagnostics. The original data generation, learner configurations, cross-fitting settings, and coverage/width-ratio evaluations are retained.

E4.justification: Table 2 adds a focused comparison of the two-dimensional predictor basis against an 11-dimensional covariate moment basis, including weight-stability diagnostics. Existing analyses of generator choice, covariate dimension, noise, correlation, and fold count remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions report 2,000 Monte Carlo replications and use 95% Wald intervals. v2 adds no new seed information, repeated-run reporting practice, or uncertainty-estimation procedure. The new ESS and CV values diagnose weight dispersion rather than uncertainty in comparative results.

E6.justification: Table 2 adds results at one retained setting: PPI++ and quadratic MEC have RMSEs 0.556 and 0.554, coverage 0.944 each, and mean CI lengths 2.171 and 2.168. Moment-basis ESS values are 86.410–89.004 versus 98.836–98.934 for MEC. Previously plotted results are unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds a formal weighted-estimating-equation framework, causal identification assumptions, an algebraic equivalence between calibrated ATE IPW and doubly robust representations, and a weighted Cox formulation. The original mean-estimation theorems and proofs are retained. Table 1 also corrects the squared-Hellinger divergence multiplier from v to sqrt(v).

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the original robustness, efficiency, and empirical claims. The conclusion now identifies a general weighted-equation formulation and two additional application examples, while explicitly stating that rigorous guarantees beyond mean estimation require further investigation.

C2.justification: Section 7 and Appendix B substantially expand discussion of applicability, richer calibration bases, and targets whose score variation offers little predictable information for efficiency gains. Section 5.1 explains the continuing dependence on labeled sample size. Appendix G.3 interprets the new comparisons and qualifies the PPI++ relationship with the N/(N+n) scaling factor.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2–B.3 supplies explicit weight-normalization instructions, source/target-set choices, and nuisance cross-fitting instructions for the extensions. The previously documented learner hyperparameters, R packages, preprocessing, and Newton-solver tolerance remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 7 and Appendix B broaden positioning from semi-supervised PPI/calibration to general estimating equations, causal inference, and survival analysis. Appendix B.4 develops explicit comparisons with TMLE, DML, generalized Oaxaca–Blinder estimation, and no-harm calibration, supported by newly added references.

P1.justification: v2 inserts an extensions section before the conclusion, adds Appendix B, and relocates the entropy discussion into it. It also adds explanatory paragraphs, notation clarifications, and an acceptance notice. Most existing prose and the original section sequence remain intact rather than being extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 adds the conceptual workflow in Figure 2 and the empirical comparison in Table 2, and reformats and relocates Table 1. Existing plots retain their graphical content, with subsequent renumbering and changes in page placement.

improvement.justification: Table 2 strengthens empirical support by evaluating the previously untested PPI++ comparator and directly examining calibration-basis choice and weight stability. The corrected Hellinger formula and clearer applicability limitations also improve accuracy and interpretation. The gains remain limited: the additional comparison covers one existing setting, and the broader causal/survival constructions receive neither empirical validation nor general efficiency guarantees, a limitation v2 explicitly acknowledges.
